slides.title: Open SetEq
slides.body: Welcome back. Last clip ended with not SetEq. Today we finally open SetEq. The textbook rule is simple. Two sets are equal when A is a subset of B and B is a subset of A. But the real question is not the rule. The real question is what the equals sign means inside a proof assistant.
slides.notes: Point at the SetEq image. Keep it casual.

slides.title: Scanner vs receipt
slides.body: Start with a tiny Lean example. n plus zero equals n closes by rfl. That means the checker can scan both sides, compute, and see the same thing. But zero plus n equals n is also true, and rfl does not close it. Now you need Nat dot zero add. So one equality was seen by the scanner, and the other needed a receipt.

slides.title: Higher sameness
slides.body: This is where the Emily Riehl idea fits. In higher category theory, you often should not ask whether two things are literally the same object. You ask whether there is a structure-preserving equivalence between them. In HoTT, equality proofs behave like paths, and univalence says an equivalence of types can be used as equality.
